name: Curator
description: Asks an LLM what your library has in common and builds the answers into ordered playlists surfaced as home screen rows.
overview: LLM-inferred vibe categories for your Jellyfin library.

versions.changelog: Fixes a bug that gave every viewer's private rows to the whole household. The nightly cleanup pass walked every stored category and rebuilt all of them for every user, so a category invented for one person was built for everyone. Measured on a live server: 102 categories, 80 of them personal, every one holding a playlist for all six users — 612 playlists where 212 belong. The run itself was always right; only the cleanup was wrong, which is why it went unnoticed until that pass became a nightly task. It repairs itself on the next cleanup: a playlist held by someone it does not belong to is removed exactly as an emptied category is, so a playlist you have untagged and taken ownership of is still never touched. Shared rows are now personalized without anyone losing one. Every viewer still gets every shared row — making them opt-in was tried and collapsed — but each viewer's own copy of the playlist is ordered for them: a favourite rises, something rated 2 out of 10 sinks, and anything they have no opinion about keeps the order the model gave it. It nudges rather than re-sorts, and because it happens inside the playlist it works in every client, including Infuse, unlike the home screen rows. OpenAI now gets a prompt cache key, so a run's calls reach the same cache — a 139,000-token prompt repeated across six calls was reporting zero cached tokens. Also in 0.5.x: Anthropic could not condense summaries at all, rejecting every batch over an empty content block; the Categories tab is rebuilt as two side-by-side cards with a sentence that reads your numbers back and warns when they contradict; scheduled tasks lost the redundant "Curator:" prefix; a Health check now button sits on the Schedule tab; each model profile carries whether it thinks; a model can optionally order each viewer's recommendation playlist; tag consolidation can optionally coin a word; the discovery pass is told what its rows are already called, after 0 of 16 then 0 of 33 names survived a run; and the distillation pass writes a run log.

The summaries era, plus everything built on it. A daily Health Check task looks for the ways Curator goes quietly wrong — runs that have stopped happening, a missing prerequisite plugin, library rows pointing at folders that no longer exist, a summary cache switched on but incomplete — and reports each with what to do about it. It reads only and costs nothing. Condensed summaries: a Summaries tab, a manual button and a daily task rewrite each long library overview into a short summary carrying its tone, cached and reused so every run sends a much smaller prompt; after the first pass only new and changed items cost anything, and your library's own overviews are never modified. The same pass optionally consolidates scraped tags, which average around eighteen values an item and are mostly production trivia. Summaries no longer end mid-phrase — measured at 11% of a real pass — because the model is asked to compose something that already fits rather than writing to the limit and stopping. Each viewer gets a recommendation playlist, ordered most recommended first, merged from the categories they already have and costing no extra model call; every viewer's copy shares one configurable name, which makes it usable as the source for a spotlight banner such as the Media Bar plugin. A daily Clean Up and Sync task reconciles categories against the playlists that actually exist, republishes home screen rows, and drops summaries for items that have left the library. Home screen rows stop flickering: a category keeps its row for a few runs when the model does not re-propose it, rather than losing it immediately and usually getting it back.

Model profiles: save several providers, models and API keys as a list and pick which one runs, instead of one set of fields you overwrite. Each profile carries its own key and its own prices, so switching profile switches the cost reporting with it — a cheap model is no longer reported at an expensive model's rate. Your existing provider, model and key migrate automatically into a single profile. Also fixes prompt caching on xAI Grok and stops under-reporting what a run costs. Grok stores cache entries on the server that wrote them, so a run's calls were scattering across the fleet and each landing on a machine that had never seen the item list; every call now carries the run's ID so they route together. Measured before the fix: 16 of 18 calls reported 128 cached tokens against a byte-identical 28,000-token prefix. Separately, cache reads were being dropped from the cost total entirely, understating one run by 24%.

Batch size 0 now sends the whole library in one request, and is the default: a thread running through items split across two batches is one the model never gets to see. The settings page is reorganised into tabs by subject, and items in collections you name — Oscar Nominees and Oscar Winners by default — are labelled as such so the model can weigh an award as evidence about a film. Also fixes personalization for anyone who watches television. Jellyfin records playback against episodes, so a series row carries no watch history and every TV viewer read as a viewer of nothing — measured on a 297-item library, six users' activity held 210 movie entries against 3 series entries. Episode playback is now rolled up onto the series and reaches the model as watch depth. Items orphaned by a removed or remounted library folder no longer reach the model: Jellyfin keeps the database row, so a ghost still looks like a real item and plays back as nothing, and on one server 36 of 298 items were such ghosts landing in real playlists. A progress panel replaces the status line that used to tell you to go read the server log, showing the phase in plain words and a breakdown of estimated cost as the run proceeds.

Requires Jellyfin 10.11.11 or newer. Adds native Google Gemini and xAI Grok providers, both constraining the model to a response schema so a malformed answer cannot lose a batch, alongside Anthropic, OpenAI and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Every run writes a complete JSON record — the settings it ran under, every step, every prompt and response in full, and cost per call and per run. Category size and count limits are told to the model as well as enforced on its answer, since a limit the model cannot see is one it cannot aim at. A renamed category keeps its playlist, its position and its watch state: models reword the same theme every run, and matching on the name alone tore down and rebuilt every home screen row each time. This is also the first release that runs at all on Jellyfin 10.11.11, which broke the plugin ABI, and it carries the earlier pipeline whole: library scan, category reconciliation, playlist building with ownership tagging, home screen rows via Collection Sections, prompt caching, an optional batch API path, a weekly scheduled task and a configuration page with a manual run button.
